source.title: AOGNets: Compositional Grammatical Architectures for Deep Learning
source.authors: Xi-Lai Li; Xi Song; Tianfu Wu

record.tranche_reason: The paper compares model interpretability across architectures using network dissection, a different measurement from the neuron-pole audit in the claim.
record.gate_note: The paper reports that AOGNet has the best network-dissection interpretability score among the compared models. It measures unique detectors in the last convolution layer, not the share of neuron poles with one or more jobs. The figure also plots detector counts, but it does not give readable exact values in the text.
record.test_reason: An architecture paper. Its only interpretability result is a network-dissection count of unique detectors in the last convolution layer, used to score its own architecture (AOGNet) against others. That is a count, not the share of interpretable units that V4 names. The count is confounded by layer width: AOGNet's last stage has 1400+ channels versus a few hundred in AlexNet or VGG. Exact values cannot be read from the text. Tools are not varied, and no claim about why late-layer neurons are messy is tested. The result fits no version, so no verdict is given.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors say AOGNet obtains the best network-dissection interpretability score, measured as unique detectors in the last conv layer. They say this shows the AOG block has potential to induce interpretability by design. Their main conclusions are about accuracy on CIFAR, ImageNet and COCO, and adversarial robustness.
record.recipe_differences: This is a vision-network architecture study using network dissection, not an audit of language-model neuron poles or tested neuron explanations.

fits_no_version.finding: AOGNet has the most unique network-dissection detectors in its last convolution layer among ImageNet-pretrained networks, from AlexNet to DenseNet (Figure 6). Counts are not normalised by layer width.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Architecture choice changes the absolute number of concept-detector units found by network dissection in the final conv layer of vision CNNs.

record.problems: The interpretability comparison is reported as a network-dissection detector score rather than the proportion of interpretable neurons; exact plotted values are not stated in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No other findings in the paper directly measure the claim versions. Classification, detection, segmentation, and adversarial-robustness results do not assess neuron-pole interpretability.

untested.parts: Share of interpretable neurons, the effect of better interpretation tools, regularization as a cause, and the InceptionV1-sized estimates (about 5% to about 99%).

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' and its V4 'supports' label are not justified: a raw detector count, not a share, confounded by width, for the authors' own architecture. The paper does not mention neuron poles, superposition or the essay's claims.

versions.untested_parts: Neuron-pole job shares across language models, dense or mixture-of-experts models, or model scales.
InceptionV1 cat-and-car example, pose detection, and recursive generalization.

rows.measure: Network-dissection interpretability score, based on unique detectors (filter kernels).
rows.value: Best score among the compared models, as stated in the text; exact value not stated.
rows.note: The text gives the result for AOGNet collectively; Figure 6 plots the AOGNet sizes separately, without readable exact values in the supplied text. This is a detector-count score, not a measured share of interpretable neuron poles.
rows.check: The measure is the number of unique network-dissection detectors, not the share of interpretable neurons. A wider last layer can raise this count without raising the share. The row is the study's own architecture compared with others, and the baseline and exact values are not stated (Figure 6 is unreadable). It cannot show V4's effect, so state 'observed' is wrong.

relation.reason: It applies the cited network-dissection metric to its own models. It does not test the claim or use it. The reader's earlier call of tests/T2 was wrong.

tranche.reason: This is an architecture paper. It uses network dissection only to score its own AOGNet against other networks, as a unique-detector count. That is a related but different construct from the share of interpretable units, so it does not test the claim.

source_check.notes: The text says only that AOGNet has the best unique-detector count in the last conv layer, with no numbers. Figure 6 also has a panel for the total number of detectors, again with no readable values. Neither is a share of interpretable units, and no verdicts are warranted.
